title: Joining commands with pipes
objectives: Chain shell commands with pipes and redirect output to a file
Find files by name with find and by contents with grep -r
Write a shell script that loops over tickers

screens.prose:
Your broker sends `trades.csv`, one trade per line. You want only the tickers. `cut` splits each line at a character you name, then keeps the pieces you ask for:

```sh
$ cut -d, -f2 trades.csv
```

`-d,` splits at commas; `-f2` keeps piece 2.

state.caption: trades.csv, each line split at its commas. The column number is the field number.

screens.question: Tap every piece this prints.

hints.text: Which column is field 2?
This is the first line of the file, and cut treats it like any other.
cut prints field 2 of all seven lines, the header line included.

feedback.correct: Field 2 of every line, header included: seven lines.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. cut keeps field 2 of every line in the file.

byKey.no-header: You skipped the header. cut does not know it is a header; it prints `ticker` too.
byKey.r0c0: That is field 1, the date. `-f2` keeps the second field.

explain.text: cut printed field 2 of each of the seven lines. The first is the word `ticker`, from the header. Remember it: it will turn up in every count we make next.

screens.prose:
Now feed those seven lines through two more commands. `sort` puts lines in order. `uniq -c` collapses repeated lines into one, with a count in front.

```sh
$ cut -d, -f2 trades.csv | sort | uniq -c
```

state.caption: trades.csv, each line split at its commas. The column number is the field number.

screens.question: What does it print?

options.text: 3 AAPL, 2 MSFT, 1 NVDA, 1 ticker (one per line)

options.why: You dropped the header line. cut passed `ticker` along, so it is counted too.

options.text: Seven lines, each with a count of 1
options.why: That is what happens without `sort`. Here sort puts equal tickers next to each other first.
You counted lines, as `wc -l` would. `uniq -c` counts each distinct line.

hints.text: After sort, which lines sit next to each other?
Field 2 holds AAPL three times and MSFT twice.
sort gives AAPL, AAPL, AAPL, MSFT, MSFT, NVDA, ticker. uniq -c then counts each run.

feedback.correct: Each command works on the output of the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the lines through cut, then sort, then uniq -c.

byKey.noheader: You dropped the header. Nothing in the chain removes it, so `1 ticker` appears.

explain.text: A chain of commands joined by pipes is a **pipeline**. cut sent seven lines, sort grouped them, and uniq -c counted each group. The stray `1 ticker` is the header, still riding along.

screens.prose:
You try to save a step and leave out `sort`:

```sh
$ cut -d, -f2 trades.csv | uniq -c
```

state.caption: trades.csv, each line split at its commas. The column number is the field number.

screens.question: How many lines does it print?

widget.label: Lines printed
widget.accept: 7: no two equal tickers sit next to each other, so nothing collapses.

hints.text: uniq only compares each line with the one just before it.
Read field 2 from top to bottom.
ticker, AAPL, MSFT, AAPL, NVDA, MSFT, AAPL: no line equals its neighbour, so all seven stay.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. uniq collapses a line only when it repeats the line just above.

byKey.same: You expected the same four counts. uniq only merges neighbours, and no two AAPL lines are neighbours here.
byKey.three: You counted the three tickers. Without sort, repeats are not next to each other, so none merge.

explain.text: uniq compares each line only with the line before it. The AAPL lines are never neighbours, so each prints with a count of 1. That is why `sort | uniq -c` is a pair.

screens.prose:
Pipes handle what is inside files. To find the files themselves, use `find`. It walks a folder and every folder inside it.

```sh
$ find . -name "*.csv"
```

state.caption: The dot means the current folder

screens.question: Tap the lines it prints.

hints.text: Which names end in .csv, in any folder?
This one sits in tests, not in data.
Four files end in .csv: two in data, one in results, one in tests.

feedback.correct: All four .csv files, wherever they sit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. find looks in every folder below the current one.

byKey.data-only: You looked in data only. find searches every folder, results and tests included.
byKey.no-tests: You missed the test's small price file. find searches tests too.

explain.text: find went into every folder and kept names matching `*.csv`. `ls *.csv` would have found nothing, since no .csv sits at the top. The quotes stop the shell expanding the star before find sees it.

screens.prose:
`grep -r` searches the **contents** of every file in every folder. With `-l` it prints only the names of files that match.

```sh
$ grep -rl momentum .
```

state.caption: A folder of five one-line files

screens.question: Tap the file names it prints.

hints.text: grep reads what is inside each file. Does the name count?
Read this file's contents closely.
momentum appears inside README.md, backtest.py and test_signal.py. momentum.py's own text never says it.

feedback.correct: Three files contain the word. The file named momentum.py does not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. grep matches what is inside the files, not their names.

byKey.by-name: You included momentum.py for its name. grep reads contents, and its one line never says momentum.
byKey.name-only: You searched by name, which is find's job. grep -r reads contents.
byKey.r2c0: You picked momentum.py for its name. Its contents never say momentum.
byKey.r4c0: notes.txt talks about mean reversion. The word momentum is not in it.

explain.text: grep -r read every file and printed the three whose text contains momentum. momentum.py matched only by name, so grep skipped it. find searches names; grep searches contents.

screens.prose:
To run a backtest over several tickers, save the commands in a script, `run_all.sh`. `START=2019-01-01` sets a variable (no spaces round `=`) and `$START` reads it. The loop runs its body once per ticker, with `T` set to it.

```sh
#!/bin/bash
START=2019-01-01
for T in SPY QQQ IWM; do
  echo "Running $T from $START"
  python3 backtest.py "$T" "$START" >> results.csv
done
```

state.caption: One line per run: the ticker and its Sharpe ratio

screens.question: You run `bash run_all.sh`. What appears on the screen?

options.text: Three lines: Running SPY from 2019-01-01, then the same for QQQ and IWM

options.why: You read the variables as plain text. Inside double quotes the shell replaces `$T` and `$START` with their values.

options.text: Six lines: each Running line, then that ticker's Sharpe ratio
options.why: You expected the Sharpe lines on screen. `>>` sends them into results.csv instead.
You expected only the last pass to show. echo runs on every pass, so each ticker prints.

hints.text: Where does each command's output go: the screen or a file?
echo prints to the screen on each pass. The backtest's line goes into results.csv because of `>>`.

feedback.correct: Three Running lines on screen; the Sharpe ratios went into the file.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow one pass of the loop, then repeat it for each ticker.

byKey.six: You expected the backtest's output on screen. `>>` redirected it to results.csv.

explain.text: Each pass sets `T`, echoes one line to the screen and appends one line to results.csv. So the screen shows three Running lines. results.csv ends with SPY,0.71, QQQ,0.88 and IWM,0.32.

screens.prose:
A colleague's version of the script uses one `>` instead of `>>`. `results.csv` starts empty.

```sh
#!/bin/bash
for T in SPY QQQ IWM; do
  python3 backtest.py "$T" > results.csv
done
```
screens.question: How many lines does `results.csv` hold afterwards?

widget.label: Lines in results.csv
widget.accept: 1: each pass empties the file and writes one line, so only IWM's survives.

hints.text: What does `>` do to a file that already has something in it?
This is the last pass of the loop.
`>` empties the file before writing. Each pass wipes the line before it, and IWM's pass is last.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what `>` does at the start of each pass.

byKey.three: You expected each pass to add a line. `>` empties the file first, every pass, so only IWM's line survives.
byKey.zero: Each pass does write a line. The last one, IWM's, is still there at the end.

explain.text: `>` empties results.csv and then writes, on every pass. SPY's line is wiped by QQQ's, and QQQ's by IWM's. Inside a loop, append with `>>`.

screens.prose:
The patterns you used:

```sh
cmd1 | cmd2           # cmd2 reads cmd1's output
cmd > file            # empty the file, then write
cmd >> file           # add to the end
find . -name "*.csv"  # by name, every folder
grep -r word .        # by contents, every folder
for T in A B C; do    # the body runs once per word,
  cmd "$T"            # with $T set to that word
done
```
screens.question: Which command adds a line to `log.txt` without erasing what is there?

options.why: You picked the single `>`. It empties log.txt first, as in the loop that kept only IWM.
A pipe feeds another command, and log.txt is a file. The shell would try to run it as a program.

hints.text: Which sign appends?
`>>` adds to the end; `>` starts the file afresh.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the loop that kept only one line.

explain.text: `>>` appends and `>` overwrites. A pipe joins two commands, never a command and a file. Mixing these up is the commonest way to lose a results file.

screens.prose: Build a pipeline that prints only the most traded ticker in `trades.csv`, with its count. `sort -rn` sorts by number, largest first. `head -n 1` keeps the first line.

state.caption: trades.csv, each line split at its commas. The column number is the field number.

screens.question: Put the pieces of the pipeline in order.

hints.text: You need counts before you can sort by count.
Cut the tickers, sort so repeats sit together, count them, sort the counts largest first, keep the top line.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each step needs the output of the one before.

byKey.uniq: uniq -c needs equal lines next to each other, so plain sort comes before it.
byKey.rn: Sort by count once the counts exist, after uniq -c.
byKey.head: Keep the top line last, once the largest count is on top.
byKey.sort: Plain sort groups the tickers, so it comes straight after cut.
byKey.cut: Start by cutting out the tickers; every other step reads them.

explain.text: The counts come out as 3 AAPL, 2 MSFT, 1 NVDA, 1 ticker. `sort -rn` keeps 3 AAPL on top, and `head -n 1` keeps that line. Without `-n`, sort would compare the counts as text, and 10 would come before 9.

screens.prose:
Your Stage 1 script now runs over five ETFs. `returns.py` prints one line: ticker, annualised volatility, maximum drawdown. You run this, spot a bug in `returns.py`, fix it and run it again.

```sh
for T in SPY QQQ IWM EFA TLT; do
  python3 returns.py "data/$T.csv" >> results.csv
done
```
screens.question: How many lines does `results.csv` hold now? It did not exist before the first run.

widget.label: Lines in results.csv
widget.accept: 10: each run appends five lines, and nothing ever empties the file.

hints.text: Does anything in the script empty the file?
`>>` only appends. Two runs of five lines each leave ten, with the stale ones first.

feedback.correct: Ten lines: five stale, then five fresh.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count what each run appends, and whether anything clears the file.

byKey.five: You expected the second run to replace the first. `>>` only appends, so the buggy five lines are still there.
byKey.one: That would happen with `>` inside the loop. With `>>`, every line is kept.

explain.text: `>>` kept the five lines from the buggy run above the five good ones. Start the script with `echo "ticker,vol,mdd" > results.csv`: one `>` before the loop clears the file and writes a header. Then every run gives one header and five fresh rows.

ideas: In a pipeline each command reads the output of the one before: `cut | sort | uniq -c` counts.
find searches every folder for names; grep -r searches every folder for contents.
A loop runs its body once per word. Inside it, append with `>>`; clear the file once, before the loop.

formula.name: Count each value in a column
formula.note: uniq only merges neighbours, so sort first.

summary.trap: `>` inside a loop empties the file on every pass. Only the last line survives.

quiz.prose:
Field 3 of `trades.csv` is the side. Its seven lines are: side, buy, sell, sell, buy, buy, buy.

```sh
$ cut -d, -f3 trades.csv | sort | uniq -c
```
quiz.question: What count is printed next to `buy`?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the buy lines.

byKey.three: You missed one. Count again: lines 2, 5, 6 and 7 say buy.
byKey.seven: That counts every line. uniq -c counts each value separately.

explain.text: sort groups the four buy lines together, then the two sells and the header. uniq -c prints 4 buy, 2 sell, 1 side.

quiz.prose: Your project has Python files at the top and inside `signals/` and `tests/`.
quiz.question: Which command lists every Python file, in every folder?

options.why: ls looks only in the current folder. The files in signals and tests are missed.
grep -r searches contents. It prints every line containing the letters py, in any file.

feedback.correct: find searches names in every folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You want names, in every folder.

explain.text: find walks down through every folder and matches names. ls stays at the top. grep reads contents, not names.

quiz.prose:
A script starts with this line:

```sh
START = 2019-01-01
```
quiz.question: What happens when it runs?

options.why: You read it like Python. In the shell, spaces round `=` turn it into a command named START.

options.text: START is set to an empty value
options.why: With the spaces, nothing is set at all. The shell tries to run START.

feedback.correct: The shell runs START as a command, with = and the date as its arguments.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shell variables allow no spaces round `=`.

explain.text: The shell splits the line at spaces, so START becomes a command name. No such command exists. Write `START=2019-01-01`, with no spaces.

quiz.prose:
Inside the loop, `T` is SPY. The script runs:

```sh
echo 'Running $T'
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: That is what double quotes give. Single quotes keep every character as typed.
The shell does not read `$T` here at all, so nothing is replaced.

feedback.correct: Single quotes print exactly what is inside them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare single and double quotes.

explain.text: Inside single quotes the shell replaces nothing. Inside double quotes it replaces `$T` with SPY. Use double quotes round variables.
